blocks.text: {blue|Two-variable data} is a set of pairs—hours studied and score earned, temperature and sales. A {teal|scatterplot} plots each pair as a point, and the cloud's shape reveals the **association** between the variables:

blocks.caption: As $x$ increases, $y$ **tends to increase**.
blocks.alt: Scatterplot with points rising from lower left to upper right

blocks.caption: As $x$ increases, $y$ **tends to decrease**.
blocks.alt: Scatterplot with points falling from upper left to lower right

blocks.caption: No trend — $x$ tells you little about $y$.
blocks.alt: Scatterplot with points scattered with no visible pattern

items: **Read the axes first**—what each variable is, and in what units. Half the wrong answers misuse the axes.
**The line of best fit summarizes the trend.** Predictions come from the **line**, not from individual points.
**Slope = predicted change in $y$ per one unit of $x$**; the y-intercept is the prediction at $x = 0$. Interpret both with the axes' units.
**Actual $-$ predicted:** a point above the line beats its prediction; below the line falls short.
**Association is a tendency, not a law**—and it is not causation. The right answers say “tends to” and “predicted.”

blocks.text: Every scatterplot question is one of four jobs: describe the trend, interpret the line's numbers, predict from the line, or compare a point with the line. Identify the job before touching the plot.
Besides its **direction**, a cloud of points has a **shape**. If the trend runs straight, a linear model fits; if it bends, you'll need a curve:

blocks.caption: Constant rate — a **line** fits.
blocks.alt: Scatterplot with points along a straight rising line

blocks.caption: Rises, peaks, falls — a **curve** fits.
blocks.alt: Scatterplot with points following an arch shape

blocks.caption: Hours of TV per day ($h$) and test score ($s$) for eight students.
blocks.alt: Scatterplot of test score versus hours of TV, with points trending downward

blocks.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship shown in the scatterplot?
choices: As TV time increases, test scores tend to decrease
As TV time increases, test scores tend to increase
There is no relationship between TV time and test scores
Watching more TV causes lower test scores

items.text: The cloud falls from left to right—a negative association, described with “tends to.”
That would slope upward; this cloud clearly falls.
“No relationship” looks like a shapeless cloud—this one has an unmistakable downward drift.
The data shows the two variables *move together*—it cannot show that one **causes** the other. Association is never causation on the SAT.

blocks.text: Correct answers about scatterplots hedge: “tend to,” “in general,” “predicted.” Choices with “causes,” “always,” or “every” overstate what data can say—and they're nearly always wrong.

The {teal|line of best fit} runs through the middle of the cloud—roughly half the points above, half below—and turns the trend into an equation you can interpret and use. Here, quiz score $y$ against hours studied $x$, fit by $\hat{y} = 4x + 55$:

blocks.caption: Hours studied vs. quiz score, with the line of best fit.
blocks.alt: Scatterplot of quiz scores rising with study hours, with a fitted line through the cloud

rows: **predicted** increase of $4$ points for each additional hour studied
**predicted** score for a student who studies $0$ hours
blocks.caption: Interpretations always carry the axes' units — points per hour, points at zero hours.

blocks.stem: Based on the model $\hat{y} = 4x + 55$, which of the following is the best interpretation of the number $4$?
choices: The predicted increase in quiz score for each additional hour studied
The predicted quiz score for a student who does not study
The number of hours a typical student studies
The exact number of points every student gains per hour of studying

items.text: The slope multiplies $x$ (hours), so it's the predicted change in $y$ (points) per one hour.
That's the y-intercept's job—the $55$.
$4$ carries units of points **per hour**, not hours—the units veto this reading.
“Exact… every student” claims certainty a trend line doesn't have. Models **predict on average**; the scattered points prove individuals vary.

blocks.text: Best-fit interpretations have a fixed grammar: slope → “predicted change in [y-units] per one [x-unit]”; intercept → “predicted [y] when [x] is zero.” Match the choice to the grammar and the units.

pages.title: Predictions & the Gap to the Line

blocks.text: To predict, feed an $x$-value to the **line**—the points have already done their job by shaping it.
Using $\hat{y} = 4x + 55$, what score does the model predict for a student who studies $6$ hours?
Real students don't land exactly on the line. The vertical gap—**actual $-$ predicted**—says who beat the model and by how much. One student studied $6$ hours and scored $85$:

blocks.caption: Actual $85$, predicted $79$: the point sits $\green{6}$ **above** the line — $6$ points better than predicted.
blocks.alt: The scatterplot with the point at 6 hours, 85 points highlighted above the fitted line, with a dashed gap of 6

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: Point **above** the line → actual $>$ predicted (difference positive). Point **below** → actual $<$ predicted (negative). “Farthest from the line” means the largest vertical gap, sign ignored.

blocks.caption: Four data points and the line of best fit $\hat{y} = x + 2$.
blocks.alt: Scatterplot with four labeled points around the line y equals x plus 2

blocks.stem: For which point does the actual $y$-value differ **most** from the value predicted by the line of best fit?
choices: A
B
C
D

items.text: Predicted $2 + 2 = 4$, actual $7$: a gap of $3$.
Predicted $7$, actual $6$: a gap of only $1$.
Predicted $10$, actual $14$: a gap of $4$—the largest vertical distance from the line.
Predicted $11$, actual $10$: a gap of $1$. Being far to the *right* isn't being far from the *line*.

blocks.text: When the SAT asks *which kind of model* fits, it's a shape-recognition task—the same fingerprints from the Nonlinear Functions lesson, now worn by data:

blocks.caption: Steady climb — equal steps.
blocks.alt: Data points along a straight line

blocks.caption: Falls, turns, rises — a vertex.
blocks.alt: Data points in a U shape

blocks.caption: Slow, then steep — multiplying.
blocks.alt: Data points rising along an exponential curve

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: From a table with equal $x$-steps: constant **differences** → linear model; constant **ratios** → exponential model; differences that shrink then grow (or a visible turn) → quadratic.

blocks.stem: The table shows values from a data set. Which type of model best fits the data?
choices: Increasing exponential
Increasing linear
Decreasing exponential
Quadratic with a minimum

items.text: Each step **doubles** $y$: ratios $\frac{6}{3} = \frac{12}{6} = \frac{24}{12} = 2$. Constant ratio, growing values—exponential growth, $y = 3 \cdot 2^x$.
Linear needs constant differences; these are $3, 6, 12$—growing, not constant.
The values rise; decay falls.
A quadratic with a minimum would fall before it rises—these values only climb, and by ratios, not by a turning pattern.

blocks.text: Growth by **adding** (“$120$ more members each year”) → linear. Growth by **multiplying** (“increases $8\%$ each year”, “doubles”) → exponential. The verbs in the question tell you the model.
Name the job—trend, interpretation, prediction, gap-to-line, or model choice—then keep units and “predicted” language in view.

blocks.caption: Outdoor temperature $t$ (°C) and cups of hot chocolate sold $c$ at a cafe on nine days.
blocks.alt: Scatterplot of hot chocolate sales versus temperature, trending downward

blocks.stem: Which statement about the data in the scatterplot is true?
choices: As temperature increases, sales tend to decrease
As temperature increases, sales tend to increase
Temperature and sales show no association
Selling less hot chocolate causes the temperature to rise

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** The cloud falls steadily from left to right—warm days, few cups.

items.text: A clear negative association, stated as a tendency. {green|✓}
The trend runs the other way.
The downward drift is unmistakable—“no association” would look like a formless cloud.
Backwards *and* causal: the data can't establish causation in either direction—it only shows the variables moving together.

blocks.stem: The model $h = 12w + 30$ predicts the height $h$, in millimeters, of a seedling $w$ weeks after planting. Which is the best interpretation of the number $12$ in this context?
choices: The predicted increase in height, in millimeters, each week
The height of the seedling, in millimeters, when it was planted
The predicted height, in millimeters, after one week
The number of weeks it takes the seedling to double in height

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** The $12$ multiplies $w$ (weeks), so its units are millimeters **per week**—the slope's predicted weekly growth.

items.text: Slope grammar: predicted change in $h$ per one unit of $w$. {green|✓}
The height at planting ($w = 0$) is the intercept, $30$.
The predicted height after one week is $12(1) + 30 = 42$ mm—the whole expression, not the $12$ alone.
$12$ is in millimeters per week, not weeks—units rule it out.

blocks.stem: A line of best fit for a data set is $\hat{y} = 3x + 20$. One of the data points is $(10, 44)$. What is the actual $y$-value **minus** the value predicted by the model at $x = 10$?

items.note: Actual minus predicted — the point sits $6$ **below** the line

items.text: Negative, because the actual value fell short of the prediction. {green|✓}
$+6$ subtracts in the wrong order—sign carries meaning here (above vs. below the line).
$44$ is the actual value alone; the question asks for the comparison.
$50$ is the predicted value alone—one input to the subtraction, not its result.

blocks.stem: Which type of model best fits the data in the table?
choices: Decreasing exponential
Decreasing linear
Increasing exponential
Quadratic with a maximum

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Each step **halves** $y$: ratios of $\frac{1}{2}$ throughout—constant ratio, shrinking values. The model is $y = 80 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^x$.

items.text: Constant ratio $\frac{40}{80} = \frac{20}{40} = \frac{10}{20} = \frac{1}{2}$. {green|✓}
Linear decay needs equal drops; these drops are $40, 20, 10$—shrinking, not constant.
The values fall; growth rises.
A quadratic with a maximum rises before it falls—this data only falls, and by ratios.

blocks.title: Things to Remember
items: Read the **axes and units** before anything else. Association: cloud rises → positive, falls → negative, formless → none.
The line of best fit is the trend's summary—**predict from the line**, not from individual points.
Slope: predicted change in $y$ per one unit of $x$. Y-intercept: predicted $y$ at $x = 0$. Interpretations must match the units and say “predicted.”
**Actual $-$ predicted**: positive above the line, negative below; “farthest from the line” = largest vertical gap.
Model choice: equal differences → linear; equal ratios → exponential; a turn (peak or valley) → quadratic.
Association is never causation, and trends are tendencies—reject choices with “causes,” “exactly,” or “every.”
